persona: Backend engineer on a pricing service; solid on complexity and reasonably deep on CPython; asking to settle a review comment.

turns.user:
Settling a review thread. Hot path:

```python
BLOCKLIST = load_blocklist()  # list[str], ~200k SKUs

def is_blocked(sku: str) -> bool:
    return sku in set(BLOCKLIST)
```

Called ~50k times per batch. Reviewer says it's fine because set membership is O(1). I know set lookup is O(1) on average, that's not the question. The question: as written, is this faster or slower than plain `sku in BLOCKLIST`?

alreadyConsidered: set membership is O(1) on average
expect.notes: As written it is slower, or at best no better: set(BLOCKLIST) is O(n) on every call (allocate a table and insert 200k strings, typically milliseconds), so each call costs at least as much as the O(n) list scan, which can also exit early on a hit. The real fix is hoisting: BLOCKSET = frozenset(BLOCKLIST) at module level, turning each of the 50k lookups into a hash probe. Re-explaining O(1) set lookup is a failure. Exact timings are not required; any given must be framed as rough.

turns.user: Right. The blocklist also gets reloaded from S3 every few minutes by a background thread that just reassigns the module global. With a frozenset, is that safe for other threads to read without a lock?

expect.notes: Yes in CPython: rebinding a module global is a single reference store and a frozenset is immutable, so a reader sees either the old or the new object, never a half-built one. The one real caveat: a caller that needs a consistent view across several lookups should read the global once into a local. A caveat about free-threaded builds is acceptable but not required; a tutorial on locks is not wanted.

notes: "Which of these two is faster" where the person has already stated the obvious point (O(1) sets). Tests answering the question actually asked and contributing the hoisting fix.

persona: Senior C++ engineer on a GIS rendering plugin; knows linkers, PIC and CMake well; hit a case where the obvious fix did not work.

Linking our plugin .so fails with:

```
/usr/bin/ld: _deps/geo-install/lib/libgeo.a(projection.cpp.o): relocation R_X86_64_32 against `.rodata' can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC
```

I know what it means in general: that object in libgeo.a wasn't compiled position-independent. What I don't get is why. The top-level CMakeLists has set(CMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE ON), and our own static libs link into the same .so fine. libgeo comes in via ExternalProject_Add (it's a CMake project).

alreadyConsidered: what the error means in general (an object in the static library was not compiled position-independent)
setting CMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE ON in the top-level CMakeLists
expect.mustContribute: The actual cause: ExternalProject_Add configures and builds the dependency as a separate CMake invocation with its own cache, so it inherits none of the parent project's variables. Pass -DCMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE=ON through CMAKE_ARGS (or CMAKE_CACHE_ARGS), and force the external project to reconfigure (clear its build/stamp directory), since an existing cache will otherwise keep the old setting.
expect.notes: Re-explaining -fPIC, or asking to see the ExternalProject_Add call, is a failure: the cause is determinable from what they said.

expect.notes: Direct comparison: FetchContent brings the dependency in at configure time via add_subdirectory, so it shares the parent's variables (this bug would not have happened) and exposes real targets; the costs are option/target-name collisions, the dependency's flags, warnings and install rules leaking into your build, and longer configures. ExternalProject remains the better fit when isolation matters (different toolchain or build type, non-CMake builds, badly behaved CMake). A recommendation for their case (usually FetchContent, or find_package against a prebuilt package) is welcome.

persona: Mid-level backend engineer at a fintech, comfortable reading Postgres query plans; settling a code-review disagreement quickly.

turns.user: Postgres 16. A colleague left a review comment insisting `SELECT COUNT(1) FROM ledger_entries WHERE ...` is faster than `COUNT(*)`. Is there anything to that in Postgres specifically?

expect.notes: No. In Postgres count(*) is the zero-argument aggregate and does not inspect column values; count(1) is count("any"), which evaluates its (constant, non-null) argument per row, so it is at best identical and if anything marginally slower. The folklore comes from other databases. Neither changes whether rows are read (index-only scans depend on the visibility map, not the argument).

turns.user: Related, same PR. To check whether a user has any orders at all: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1` and test > 0 in the app, versus `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1)`. There's a btree on orders(user_id). Which one?

expect.notes: EXISTS: it stops at the first matching row, whereas COUNT(*) must visit every matching index entry (and the heap for visibility unless an index-only scan applies). Negligible for users with a handful of orders; large, and growing with order count, for heavy users. A LIMIT 1 probe is equivalent to EXISTS.

notes: Two "which is faster" questions with crisp, well-established answers. Nothing to add beyond a correct, brief answer.

persona: Security consultant writing up a penetration-test report; precise, knows TLS well, wants a fact confirmed and wording she can paste.

alreadyConsidered: the endpoint has been confirmed to negotiate only TLS 1.3
expect.notes: Correct: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed static RSA (and static DH) key exchange; key exchange is (EC)DHE, PSK, or PSK with (EC)DHE. The RSA certificate is used only for authentication (RSA-PSS signatures in the handshake). The finding is a scanner false positive, most likely conflating the RSA certificate/signature with key exchange. Suggesting she check whether TLS 1.2 is enabled is redundant: she confirmed it is not.

turns.user: Good. Separate finding: they have 0-RTT enabled. Is 0-RTT data forward secret? One precise sentence for the report.

expect.notes: No: 0-RTT early data is encrypted under keys derived solely from the resumption PSK, so it is not forward secret against compromise of that PSK (or of the server's session-ticket key), and it is also replayable; data sent after the handshake completes with psk_dhe_ke is forward secret. She asked for one sentence: the reply should contain one, not an essay.

notes: Crisp protocol facts from an expert who has already done the obvious check. Tests confident, precise answers with no redundant suggestions.

persona: Freelance science journalist fact-checking her own feature on brain-computer interfaces for a general-interest magazine; wants a defensible number and a sense of how solid it is.

turns.user: Fact-checking my own piece. I wrote 'the human brain has 100 billion neurons.' Is that right?

expect.mustContribute: The better-supported figure is about 86 billion (86 ± 8 billion), from Azevedo, Herculano-Houzel and colleagues (2009) using the isotropic fractionator, with roughly 16 billion in the cerebral cortex and 69 billion in the cerebellum. '100 billion' is an old round number that was never actually counted. Concrete caveat: the 86 billion comes from a small sample (four adult male brains), so individual and sex differences are not well characterised.
expect.notes: Give the corrected figure and a usable wording ("about 86 billion"); the uncertainty must be specific, not a generic hedge.

turns.user: And synapses? I've seen '100 trillion' in one source and 'a quadrillion' in another.

expect.mustContribute: Synapse totals are extrapolations known only to about an order of magnitude (~10^14–10^15). Stereological counts put the neocortex alone around 1.5 × 10^14 (Pakkenberg and colleagues, 2003); whole-brain figures depend on how density estimates are extrapolated across regions, and counts change with age. So '100 trillion' is defensible as a lower-end order of magnitude and 'a quadrillion' is the high end; 'hundreds of trillions' or 'on the order of 100 trillion' is the safest wording.
expect.notes: An "it depends" answer with the actual dependence (method, region, extrapolation, age) and a recommended wording, not a refusal to pick.

notes: Factual check where the popular number is wrong and the follow-up is genuinely uncertain. Tests correcting cleanly and giving calibrated uncertainty with a usable recommendation.

persona: Helen Achebe, former management consultant who writes a weekly behavioural-economics newsletter. Careful about citations, on deadline, away from her bookshelf.

turns.user: Citation check for this week's newsletter. I'm quoting the Linda problem from Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011, the FSG hardcover). What page is it on? I need 'p. X' for the footnote and the book is at the office.

expect.mustContribute: Says plainly that it cannot reliably give the page number from memory, instead of inventing one, and gives what it can: the Linda problem is in chapter 15, 'Linda: Less Is More' (Part II); the page can be checked in a minute with Google Books or Amazon's Look Inside search on the hardcover, or cited by chapter; the primary source is Tversky and Kahneman (1983), 'Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment', Psychological Review 90(4), 293–315, which a careful essay may prefer to cite.
expect.notes: Tests "I don't know" as the honest core of a useful answer. A specific page number stated as fact is the failure; a number offered only as an explicitly unverified guess is weak but not a failure. No question back about which edition: she named it.

turns.user: Fine, I'll cite the chapter and the 1983 paper. Last thing: my draft sentence is 'The Linda problem proves that people simply can't reason about probability.' OK to run?

expect.mustContribute: No: the sentence overclaims. The result shows a robust conjunction error under one framing, not a general inability: the error rate drops sharply when the problem is posed in frequencies ('of 100 people like Linda, how many…'), and part of the effect is attributed to how people read 'probable' (as 'plausible' or 'fits the description') and to conversational implicature, a long-running debate (Gigerenzer; Hertwig and Gigerenzer 1999). Offers a defensible wording, e.g. that people's intuitive judgments of likelihood can violate a basic rule of probability even when they know the rule.
expect.notes: She owns the essay; a one-line suggested wording is fine because she asked whether the sentence can run.

notes: A citation request whose honest answer is "I don't know that detail", paired with the useful partial and the primary source; then an overclaim in her own draft that deserves a plain challenge. Tests not fabricating precision and not hedging into uselessness.
